# Piecewise Linear Mapping and Integration


## Overview
This family provides methods to map scalar volume data to opacity and integrate these values along viewing rays using piecewise linear approximations. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the volume rendering integral while allowing for flexible, user-defined opacity mappings that can be linearly interpolated between control points. It differs from its siblings by focusing on the structural linearity of the transfer function or the density field to enable analytical integration or simple interpolation, whereas [Alpha-to-Weight Computation (Forward)](2373-alpha-to-weight-computation-forward.md) focuses on weight computation and [SDF-based Opacity Derivation via Logistic CDF](3233-sdf-based-opacity-derivation-via-logistic-cdf.md) uses probabilistic models.

## Shared principles
The family operates on the scalar field $V(\mathbf{p})$ sampled at positions $\mathbf{p}$ along the ray. The core mechanism involves a transfer function $T$ that maps the scalar value to a color vector $\mathbf{c} \in [0,1]^3$ and an opacity scalar $\alpha \in [0,1]$:
$$ T: V \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha) $$
These values are subsequently used in the front-to-back compositing equation defined in [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md). Transfer functions are typically parameterized by control points $(V_k, \mathbf{c}_k, \alpha_k)$ with interpolation between points [S2, 2789, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Piecewise Density Approximation for Reparameterized Sampling](1139-piecewise-density-approximation-for-reparameterized-sampling.md)
Piecewise Density Approximation for Reparameterized Sampling is a method for generating volume samples along a ray by approximating the density field $\sigma_r(t)$ as either piecewise constant or piecewise linear on a predefined grid. This approximation allows the cumulative opacity integral to be computed analytically, enabling the inversion of the opacity function to determine sample locations corresponding to uniform random numbers. It differs from its siblings by operating on the density field directly to facilitate analytical integration, whereas [Linear Opacity Interpolation](7016-linear-opacity-interpolation.md) interpolates opacity values directly, and [Piecewise Linear Opacity Mapping with Gradient Scaling](1335-piecewise-linear-opacity-mapping-with-gradient-scaling.md) incorporates gradient-based scaling into the opacity mapping process.

### [Piecewise Linear Opacity Mapping with Gradient Scaling](1335-piecewise-linear-opacity-mapping-with-gradient-scaling.md)
This method maps scalar volume values to opacity using piecewise linear functions defined by tissue types, then scales the resulting opacity by the magnitude of the local gradient vector to suppress tissue interiors and enhance bounding surfaces. It addresses the limitation of binary classification, which creates holes for thin structures, by ensuring all voxels map to non-zero opacity, rendering thin regions as faint wisps. It sets itself apart from [Linear Opacity Interpolation](7016-linear-opacity-interpolation.md) by explicitly incorporating gradient magnitude to modulate opacity based on local data variation, thereby enhancing edge details.

### [Linear Opacity Interpolation](7016-linear-opacity-interpolation.md)
Linear Opacity Interpolation maps scalar volume data values to opacity using linear interpolation between two threshold values. It solves the problem of isolating objects of interest by assigning high opacity to grey values inside the object and low or zero opacity to surrounding values. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using simple linear interpolation between two thresholds, whereas [Piecewise Function Scalar Opacity Transfer](12435-piecewise-function-scalar-opacity-transfer.md) supports arbitrary piecewise definitions and [Piecewise Linear Opacity Mapping with Gradient Scaling](1335-piecewise-linear-opacity-mapping-with-gradient-scaling.md) incorporates gradient information.

#### Power Function Opacity Transfer
- **Definition**: A simple power function used to map voxel values to opacity before enhancement. It allows illustrative enhancements to supplement existing volume rendering mechanisms [S1].
- **Step**: Calculate the gradient used for enhancement from the dataset *after* the simple power function transfer function has been applied, as this gradient is more effective in capturing subtle features [S1].
- **Formula**: $o_v = (k_{os}v_i)^{k_{oe}}$, where $v_i$ is the volume sample value, $k_{os}$ is the scalar controlling maximum opacity, and $k_{oe}$ is the exponent [S1].
- **Parameters**: $k_{os}$ controls maximum opacity; $k_{oe}$ controls contrast. Values of $k_{oe} < 1$ soften volume differences; values $> 1$ increase contrast [S1].

#### Piecewise Linear Transfer Function Integration
- **Definition**: A rendering technique that integrates piecewise linear transfer functions using a 2D texture map to compute correct exponential per-pixel opacity [S2, unofficial].
- **Parameters**: Texture Map: A 2D texture map parameterized by opacity and thickness [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of piecewise linear transfer functions has been widely adopted in volume rendering to provide intuitive control over visualization parameters. The integration of these functions, particularly using hardware-accelerated texture lookups for exponential opacity calculations, was highlighted in surveys of GPU-based volume rendering of unstructured grids [S2, unofficial]. The use of power functions for opacity mapping to enhance gradient-based features was introduced in early volume illustration work [S1].
